4 Magnetically responsive anisotropy

To validate the key steps in the design of the magnetically responsive anisotropy module, we carried out expression, purification, and fluorescence-based binding experiments for a magnetic-nanoparticle-binding protein. We first obtained a recombinant fusion protein containing the Fe3O4-binding peptide TVNFKLY and completed its expression, purification, and desalting. We then examined its binding to magnetic nanoparticles through FITC fluorescence labeling, co-incubation with the particles, magnetic separation, and washing, thereby providing an experimental basis for subsequently introducing magnetic-field-induced orientation into a SELP hydrogel.

4.1 Design of the Magnetic-Nanoparticle-Binding Protein

Experiment

The Fe3O4-binding capability of TVNFKLY has previously been validated through phage-display screening and multiple characterization methods [1]. We used TVNFKLY as the functional peptide in the experimental group and included GTWSLLL, which was expected not to bind magnetic nanoparticles, as a control to evaluate the contribution of the TVNFKLY sequence to particle binding. The experimental construct contained a His tag, a SUMO tag, a DogTag sequence, and the TVNFKLY peptide. The His tag was used for subsequent affinity purification, the SUMO tag helped improve soluble expression and stability of the heterologous protein [2], and DogTag provided an interface for subsequent connection to other protein modules [3,4].

Because this plasmid differs from the corresponding SUMO-DogTag plasmid by only 81 bp, we used a site-directed mutagenesis system for construction. The SUMO-DogTag plasmid was used as the backbone, and the TVNFKLY-coding sequence was introduced by high-fidelity PCR. The methylated parental template was then digested with DpnI, and Exnase II-mediated homologous recombination was used to recircularize the linear amplification product. The recombinant product was transformed into Trelief 5alpha competent cells, and single colonies were picked after selection on kanamycin-containing medium. Candidate clones were screened by colony PCR, and positive clones were further subjected to plasmid extraction and Sanger sequencing.

Results

Western blot results showed that, after IPTG addition, an enhanced band appeared in the molecular-weight region corresponding to the target fusion protein, indicating that pET28a-SUMO-DogTag-TVNFKLY could be expressed in BL21(DE3). Based on the literature and preliminary screening results, the band in the target region was relatively clear under the 1 mM IPTG condition, and this condition was therefore selected for scale-up expression [5].

We constructed an expression plasmid encoding 6xHis-SUMO-DogTag-TVNFKLY (Figure 4.1.2).

Single colonies suitable for subsequent screening were obtained on the transformation plates. In the colony PCR assay, multiple candidate clones exhibited the target band indicated in the original experimental records.

Agarose gel electrophoresis of the colony PCR products revealed a band at approximately 5,683 bp, consistent with the theoretical value (Figure 4.1.3). Sequencing results matched the designed sequence; therefore, the construct was advanced to expression validation.

4.2 Expression, Purification, and Concentration of the Fusion Protein

Experiment

The sequence-confirmed pET28a-SUMO-DogTag-TVNFKLY plasmid was transformed into E. coli BL21(DE3) competent cells, and expression strains were selected on kanamycin-containing medium. A single colony was picked for small-scale culture, and IPTG was added under different induction conditions to induce fusion-protein expression. After induction, the cells were collected and lysed, and Western blotting was used to compare changes in the protein bands before and after induction or under different induction conditions. Based on the small-scale expression-screening results, the condition showing a more prominent band in the target molecular-weight region was selected for subsequent scale-up culture. In this stage, 1 mM IPTG was ultimately used to induce expression of the fusion protein.

After scale-up culture, the cells were collected, resuspended, and disrupted by sonication to obtain the lysate. The N-terminal 6xHis tag of the fusion protein was used for Ni-affinity chromatography. The lysate, flow-through, wash, and elution fractions were collected sequentially, and enrichment of the target protein was evaluated by SDS-PAGE.

The purified elution fraction was further dialyzed or desalted to reduce the effects of imidazole, salt ions, and other small molecules on FITC labeling and subsequent particle-binding experiments. The desalted protein was concentrated using an ultrafiltration device. Samples before concentration, the retentate after concentration, and the filtrate were retained, and their protein concentrations were measured using the BCA assay.

Results

SDS-PAGE showed a relatively distinct enriched band in the approximately 25-35 kDa region of the elution fraction, whereas some contaminating proteins were mainly present in the lysate, flow-through, or wash fractions. These results indicated that Ni-affinity chromatography enriched the His-tagged SUMO-DogTag-TVN fusion protein.

The BCA results showed that the calculated protein concentration increased from approximately 0.37 mg/mL before concentration to approximately 5.04 mg/mL after concentration, indicating that ultrafiltration markedly increased the protein concentration in the retentate. A protein signal of approximately 0.34 mg/mL was still detected in the filtrate, suggesting that small-molecule interference, membrane permeation loss, or measurement background may have been present during the concentration process.

4.3 Ligation Reaction

Experiment

To verify whether the purified SUMO-DogTag-TVN fusion protein retained DogTag-mediated conjugation activity, we used GFP-SnoopTag2 as a visual reporter protein and SnoopLigase2 to catalyze covalent ligation between DogTag and SnoopTag2. The reaction systems contained either SUMO-DogTag-TVN or SUMO-DogTag lacking TVNFKLY. A negative control lacking SnoopLigase2 was also included to exclude higher-molecular-weight bands caused by protein mixing or nonspecific aggregation. Each group was reacted at room temperature for 15 min or 6 h. After the reaction, SDS-PAGE loading buffer was added to terminate the reaction, and SDS-PAGE was used to compare the migration patterns of the substrate bands and the ligation-product bands.

Results

In the control group without SnoopLigase2, GFP-SnoopTag2 and SUMO-DogTag-TVN primarily retained their respective substrate bands, and no obvious higher-molecular-weight ligation product was observed. After SnoopLigase2 was added, a new higher-molecular-weight band appeared above the substrate bands. Its migration position was consistent with the expected molecular weight of the ligation product formed by GFP-SnoopTag2 and the DogTag-containing protein.

SUMO-DogTag-TVN and SUMO-DogTag both showed the same type of enzyme-dependent band change, indicating that introduction of the TVNFKLY peptide did not substantially disrupt the ligation function of DogTag. A ligation product could already be observed after 15 min, and the corresponding band remained detectable after extending the reaction to 6 h.

Therefore, these results support the conclusion that the purified SUMO-DogTag-TVN retained detectable SnoopLigase2-dependent conjugation activity.

4.4 Functional Validation

4.4.1 FITC Fluorescence Labeling
Experiment

To track the distribution of the fusion protein during magnetic-nanoparticle incubation, magnetic separation, and washing, we fluorescently labeled the purified protein with fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC).

The protein was placed in a carbonate buffer suitable for the reaction between FITC and protein amino groups. FITC was slowly added under light-protected conditions, and the labeling reaction was allowed to proceed. After the reaction, glycine was added to terminate the remaining FITC-labeling reaction, and unreacted free dye was removed using a desalting column [6]. The control protein was subjected to the same labeling and post-treatment procedures.

Small amounts of FITC-labeled protein and unlabeled protein were analyzed by SDS-PAGE. The nonfluorescent half of the gel was immersed in Coomassie Brilliant Blue G250 rapid staining solution, while the side containing the FITC-labeled protein was kept protected from light and was not stained. Images were acquired using the 532 nm and 302 nm imaging channels. One portion was used to observe protein migration and loading, and the other was used to compare the fluorescence signals of the labeled and unlabeled samples.

Results

Gel imaging showed a clear fluorescence signal in the FITC-labeled protein lane, whereas the unlabeled protein lane displayed only weak background. The fluorescence signal largely corresponded to the protein-band region, supporting the conclusion that FITC was associated with the protein sample rather than that the signal was produced entirely by free dye in the gel.

These results indicate that the labeled fusion protein had a fluorescence signal suitable for subsequent microscopic observation.

4.4.2 Magnetic-Nanoparticle Binding and Washing
Experiment

To preliminarily evaluate the binding of SUMO-DogTag-TVN to magnetic nanoparticles and its retention after washing, the FITC-labeled fusion protein was co-incubated with Fe3O4 magnetic nanoparticles. The experimental group used the fusion protein containing TVNFKLY, whereas the control group used the control protein containing GTWSLLL. Protein input, particle amount, incubation time, and buffer system were kept as consistent as possible.

A magnetic separator was used to collect the magnetic nanoparticles and remove the original dispersion medium. The labeled-protein reaction mixture was then added and thoroughly resuspended. Co-incubation was performed at room temperature in the dark, with periodic gentle mixing to ensure sufficient contact between the protein and the particles.

After incubation, the magnetic nanoparticles were collected using the magnetic rack and the supernatant was removed. The particles were then washed multiple times with buffer to reduce the retention of unbound protein and free fluorescent material. After washing, the particles were gently resuspended, and bright-field and green-fluorescence images were acquired to determine whether the fluorescence signal remained associated with the particle fraction.

Results

After magnetic separation and multiple washes, green fluorescence could still be observed in particles or particle-aggregation regions in some microscopic fields, indicating that FITC-labeled material could be retained with the magnetic-particle fraction in this experimental workflow. Under the action of the magnetic field, the magnetic nanoparticles changed from a disordered state to an ordered arrangement, and the green fluorescence aligned accordingly. This result provided qualitative evidence for magnetic-field-guided changes in SELP orientation [7].

4.5 In Vitro Cytocompatibility of the Functional Peptide

Experiment

Reduction of WST-8 produces a water-soluble formazan signal and has been established as a colorimetric indicator of cell viability [7]. The assay was used here as a preliminary measure of peptide cytocompatibility.

Cells were treated with 5 or 10 µM functional peptide for 24, 48, or 72 h. A CCK-8 assay was used to assess relative cell viability, with control, blank, and peptide-treated groups included in the experimental design (Figure 4.5.1A).

Results

At 24 h, relative cell viability was approximately 70% in the 5 µM group and 55% in the 10 µM group. At 48 h, the values were approximately 85%–90% in both groups and were approximately 85%–95% at 72 h (Figure 4.5.1B). At both concentrations, the measured values were lower at 24 h than at the later time points.

The relatively high cell viability observed at 48 and 72 h provides preliminary evidence of limited cytotoxicity of the functional peptide at these later time points under the tested conditions, supporting its potential cytocompatibility. However, the reduced viability at 24 h indicates that early cellular responses require further evaluation before conclusions about overall cytocompatibility can be drawn.
